name: Quadratus of Athens
role: Christian apologist (defender of the faith); possibly a bishop of Athens

born.place: Unknown; probably Asia Minor or Athens

summary: Author of the earliest known Christian apology, a written defense of the faith presented to Emperor Hadrian around 125. Only a single sentence survives. He is counted with both the Apostolic Fathers and the later Apologists.

key_dates.label: Presents his apology to Emperor Hadrian (c. 124–125)

accomplishments.text: Wrote the first known Christian apology, a defense of Christianity addressed to Emperor Hadrian, beginning the tradition of 2nd-century apologetic writing.
His one surviving fragment, preserved by Eusebius, says that some of those Jesus healed or raised from the dead had lived on "even to our own times."
Eusebius reports that his apology was still in circulation in Eusebius's own day, about two centuries later.
Some scholars have suggested that the anonymous Epistle to Diognetus may be his lost apology, but this is unproven.

persecution_note: No reliable record of persecution of Quadratus survives. Later traditions about him combine several different men named Quadratus (an apologist, a prophet, and a bishop of Athens), and they cannot be confirmed. His apology may have been written in response to hostility toward Christians.
excommunication_note: No excommunication or condemnation of him is recorded.

sources.citation: Michael W. Holmes, ed. and trans., The Apostolic Fathers: Greek Texts and English Translations, 3rd ed. (Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2007).
Eusebius, The History of the Church, trans. G. A. Williamson, rev. Andrew Louth (London: Penguin, 1989). Written c. 300–325.
Robert M. Grant, Greek Apologists of the Second Century (Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1988).
